prompt: Of the four numbers read off a request profile, which one does a Flex Consumption bill follow, with the instance size and the billed duration fixed?
hint: On demand, Flex bills memory while executing and the executions themselves.

choices.text: The volume
choices.why: Right. Each request is billed the same GB-seconds and one execution, so the bill is the volume times a price per request.

choices.text: The peak hour
choices.why: The peak sizes machines, replicas and nodes. Functions adds instances as requests arrive and pays for none in advance.

choices.text: The number of idle hours
choices.why: An idle hour costs a function nothing, so it is where Functions gains, but it does not set the bill.

choices.text: The hour the traffic starts
choices.why: A function is billed the same at 03:00 as at 15:00.

prompt: A service takes 20 requests a second for 12 hours a day and none in the other 12. Over the average month of 730 hours (30.42 days), how many requests is that, in millions, to two decimal places?
hint: Requests a day, then times 730 / 24.

prompt: The shop's API is Python. At its evening peak of 80 requests a second, each taking 100 ms, how many Flex Consumption instances does it occupy with the default HTTP concurrency, and why?
hint: Requests in flight are the rate times the duration; then ask how many each instance takes.

choices.text: One, because a 2,048 MB instance takes 16 requests at once
choices.why: 16 is the default for a 2,048 MB instance in other languages. Microsoft's documentation sets Python apps to one.

choices.text: Eight: 80 × 0.1 s are in flight, one per instance
choices.why: Right. Concurrency is the rate times the duration, and a Python app takes one HTTP request per instance by default.

choices.text: Eighty, one for each request that arrives in a second
choices.why: A request lasts a tenth of a second, so the eighty of one second are not all in flight together.

choices.text: Two, the floor the program keeps for every option
choices.why: `LEAST` applies to machines, replicas and nodes. Functions on demand keeps no floor.

prompt: The number of requests in flight at once is the rate of requests multiplied by their ___.
hint: 60 a second at 100 ms each is six at once.

prompt: Match each number read off a request profile to the part of the bill it drives.
hint: Which meter or which sizing decision does each one feed?

pairs.right: Functions' executions, and Container Apps' request charge
how many machines, replicas or nodes must run
where a replica pays the idle rate, or nothing at zero
the GB-seconds, and which timeouts apply

right_distractors: the tax rate of the region

prompt: In `compare.py`'s table, two virtual machines cost 146.00, the App Service plan 219.00 and AKS 511.00 on every row, from 0.13 million requests to 1,051 million. Why?
hint: What do those three bill for, and does any profile need more of it?

choices.text: The program has a bug and ignores the profile for them
choices.why: It sizes them per hour with `copies`; the profiles simply never ask for more than the floor.

choices.text: Reservations are applied to them automatically
choices.why: No discount is in the file; the program uses pay-as-you-go rates for all three.

choices.text: Each is a fixed count of machines paid by the hour, and no profile outgrows the floor
choices.why: Right. Even busy fits two `D2s_v5` exactly, so the bill does not move with the traffic.

choices.text: Their rates are documented by Microsoft, unlike the others
choices.why: Every rate in `rates.json` is illustrative; only the Container Apps grants are documented.

prompt: The webhook profile, one call every twenty seconds all day, costs 6.89 USD on Functions and 58.75 on Container Apps. What makes the difference?
hint: Count the idle hours, then think about what each meter counts.

choices.text: Container Apps charges for every request, and Functions does not
choices.why: Container Apps' first two million requests a month are free, and the webhook makes 0.13 million.

choices.text: Functions has larger free grants than Container Apps
choices.why: The program leaves Functions' grants at zero; the difference is there without them.

choices.text: A replica cannot take a request that arrives every twenty seconds
choices.why: It can, easily; the problem is that it is paid for in between.

choices.text: No hour is idle, so replicas bill as active all month
choices.why: Right. A call in every hour keeps the replicas active; Flex pays for 131,400 seconds and nothing else.

prompt: With `CA_MIN` set to 0, which rows of the Container Apps column fell because hours with no request now cost nothing? Choose all that apply.
hint: Some rows fell for a different reason: they lost their second replica.

choices.text: nightly, from 15.82 to 0.43
choices.why: Right. Its 22 silent hours cost nothing, and the two busy ones fit inside the grants.

choices.text: steady, from 89.49 to 57.95
choices.why: Steady has no silent hour. It fell because 30 a second needs only one replica once there is no floor of two.

choices.text: office, from 52.04 to 42.18
choices.why: Right. Its fifteen silent hours went from the idle rate to nothing.

choices.text: webhook, from 58.75 to 27.22
choices.why: It never reaches zero: a call every twenty seconds keeps one replica up. It lost the second replica, not its idle hours.

choices.text: busy, which fell with the others
choices.why: Busy did not move: 667.65 both times, since eight replicas run all day either way.

prompt: At the file's rates, 0.000026 USD per GB-second and 0.40 USD per million executions, with each request billed as one second, how many millions of requests a month make a 512 MB Flex instance cost what two virtual machines cost, 146.00 USD? Two decimal places.
hint: A request costs 0.5 GB-seconds plus one execution; divide 146 by that.

prompt: Which of these does `compare.py` leave out, so that a close result between two virtual machines and Container Apps leans further towards Container Apps than the table shows?
hint: Which of the two needs something in front of it that the other brings along?

choices.text: The free grants of Container Apps
choices.why: They are in the program, taken from the active seconds.

choices.text: Reservations, which a steady load rewards
choices.why: Those would favour the machines, not Container Apps.

choices.text: The 300 seconds Container Apps waits before removing replicas
choices.why: That makes real replicas run a little longer than the program counts, which adds to Container Apps' side.

choices.text: The load balancer or gateway the machines need in front
choices.why: Right. Container Apps comes with its own ingress, and two machines need a load balancer or an Application Gateway that is not on the file.

prompt: Two copies of `shop:1.0` run on ports 8081 and 8082. An order posted to 8081 appears in its list, and 8082 answers `[]`. Why?
hint: Where does `app.py` keep its orders?

choices.text: Each process keeps its own `ORDERS` list in memory
choices.why: Right. Nothing is shared between processes, which is also why the restart emptied the first one.

choices.text: The second container had not started yet
choices.why: It answered, with an empty list; a container that had not started would not answer at all.

choices.text: The order was written to the first container's disk
choices.why: `app.py` writes nothing to disk; the list is a Python variable.

choices.text: Docker isolates the two networks, so the order could not reach 8082
choices.why: The order was never sent to 8082. Nothing in the shop forwards an order to another copy.

prompt: The month's finance export takes five minutes while the page waits. Which change lets it run behind Container Apps, App Service or Functions?
hint: Two of the three limits are not the timeout you set.

choices.text: Make it a job that finance collects when it is ready
choices.why: Right. Nothing waits on an open request, so no front end's limit applies.

choices.text: Set `functionTimeout` in `host.json` to ten minutes
choices.why: An HTTP function still has 230 seconds to answer, whatever its timeout says.

choices.text: Move it to App Service, which has no request limit
choices.why: The same 230 seconds applies, the idle timeout of the load balancer in front.

choices.text: Keep it on Container Apps, whose ingress waits longer than five minutes
choices.why: The ingress documentation gives 240 seconds, which five minutes exceed.

prompt: Put in order what happens once the month's export is a job, from finance pressing the button to the file in their hands.
items: The page puts a message on a Service Bus queue and answers at once
The message starts an event-driven Container Apps job
The job builds the file and writes it to storage
Finance collects the file when the page says it is ready
trap: Starting the job before the message exists: an event-driven job is started by the message, so the queue comes first.

prompt: The shop keeps a pool of 20 database connections per process. Moved to Flex Consumption as a Python app, why is the database the first thing to fall over in a burst?
hint: Count processes, not requests.

choices.text: Functions closes every connection after each request
choices.why: Connections can be kept by a client created outside the handler; the number of instances is the problem.

choices.text: Flex Consumption cannot reach a database in a virtual network
choices.why: It can: virtual network integration is one of Flex's additions over the old Consumption plan.

choices.text: The 230-second limit holds connections open too long
choices.why: The limit is on answering a request; it says nothing about how many connections exist.

choices.text: Every request in flight is an instance with its own pool
choices.why: Right. One HTTP request per instance by default means a burst to 100 instances is 100 pools.

prompt: Of these moves, which asks the least of the shop's code?
hint: Which two targets run the same image?

choices.text: From Container Apps to Functions on Flex
choices.why: The web server has to become handlers in `function_app.py`, which is the dearest move in the table.

choices.text: From one virtual machine to two, behind a load balancer
choices.why: The code runs unchanged, but the orders in memory still have to move to a database first.

choices.text: From Container Apps to AKS
choices.why: Right. The same `shop:1.0` runs in both; the move is new manifests around it.

choices.text: From one virtual machine to Container Apps
choices.why: It needs the statelessness the others need, plus the image, which the shop happens to have.

prompt: The shop's profile peaks at 80 requests a second. Why does that peak cost Container Apps almost nothing extra?
hint: How many replicas does 80 need, and how many run anyway?

choices.text: The peak lasts only two hours, which are free
choices.why: Nothing about an evening hour is free; the grants are a monthly total.

choices.text: 80 needs two replicas of 50, and two run anyway
choices.why: Right. Only four hours exceed what one replica carries, and the floor already covers them.

choices.text: Container Apps does not bill for requests at the peak
choices.why: It bills requests past two million a month whenever they arrive.

choices.text: Scale-out is faster than scale-in
choices.why: True of KEDA, and it changes nothing in the program's bill.

prompt: At the file's active rates, 0.00002 USD per vCPU-second and 0.000002 per GiB-second, what does a nightly report cost a month as a Container Apps job of 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB that runs 12 minutes a night, over 30.42 nights, with the grants already spent? USD, two decimal places.
hint: 720 seconds a night, times the nights, times each resource and its rate.

prompt: The same shop profile with silent nights costs 69.34 USD on Container Apps instead of 85.81. What paid for the 16.47 difference?
hint: Compare the two profiles hour by hour.

choices.text: The request charge on the requests the trickle sends
choices.why: The trickle is 1.75 million requests a month; at 0.40 a million that is under a dollar.

choices.text: Two replicas kept at the active rate all night
choices.why: Right. The trickle of 2 a second keeps both replicas off the idle rate all night.

choices.text: A third replica that the trickle starts every night
choices.why: Two requests a second fit in one replica; the floor is two and stays two.

choices.text: Cold starts that the trickle triggers
choices.why: With a minimum of two, nothing starts cold; and a cold start is not on the program's bill.

prompt: A decision like the shop's is only finished when it names the numbers that would ___ it.
hint: Traffic three times today's is one of them.

prompt: At three times today's traffic, two virtual machines cost 146.00 and Container Apps 159.92. What does that tell the shop?
hint: Is a 10% gap at illustrative rates a verdict?

choices.text: To move to virtual machines now, before the traffic grows
choices.why: Today Container Apps is 60.19 cheaper; the crossing is a trigger to watch, not a date.

choices.text: That Container Apps stops scaling past 240 requests a second
choices.why: It scales to five replicas there; the program prices them, which is how the total grew.

choices.text: That growth near that size reopens the decision, and the real rates have to settle it
choices.why: Right. Within 20% is a tie even at real rates, and these are illustrative; it is where to price machines properly.

choices.text: That the free grants run out at that volume
choices.why: The grants are spent by today's traffic already; tripling it adds replicas and requests.

prompt: Match each of the shop's workloads, and the webhook of section 02, to where this lesson runs it.
hint: Think of who waits, how long the work runs and how often it is called.

pairs.right: a Container App with a minimum of two replicas
an event-driven job started from a queue

right_distractors: an AKS cluster on the Standard tier

prompt: Put the lesson's method in order, from the traffic to the decision.
items: Write the traffic down as 24 hourly rates
Read the volume, the peak, the idle hours and the duration
Price the profile five ways with the rates in a file
Check the limits and what the code assumes
Write the decision down with what would reopen it
trap: Pricing before reading the profile: the program needs the profile as its input, so the numbers come first.

prompt: At the file's active rates, 0.00002 USD per vCPU-second and 0.000002 per GiB-second, what does one Container Apps replica of 0.5 vCPU and 1 GiB cost when it is active for a whole 730-hour month, before any free grant? USD, two decimal places.
hint: 730 × 3,600 seconds, times 0.5 vCPU at one rate and 1 GiB at the other.

prompt: A new internal stock page follows the office profile, is written in Python, and nobody minds a slow first answer in the morning. The team knows containers. Which fits it best, by this lesson's method?
hint: Fifteen silent hours, nobody waiting, and an image the team can build.

choices.text: Container Apps, scaled to zero
choices.why: Right. 42.18 in the zero run, the silent hours free, and the cold start lands on nobody who minds.

choices.text: Two virtual machines, the simplest move
choices.why: 146.00 a month for a tool that is silent fifteen hours a day, plus the operating system to look after.

choices.text: Functions on Flex, since it pays nothing while idle
choices.why: Idle is free, but 59.13 million requests at one billed second each cost 3,098.41 at the file's rates.

choices.text: A small AKS cluster on the Free tier
choices.why: Three nodes still run all night, and the cluster is a second thing to operate for one page.
